summary: This Wikipedia article gives an overview of the Armenian people, covering their religious history, including the two Catholicosates established in 1441, and their political history from brief independence (1918-1920) through Soviet rule to independence in 1991. It also describes the early development of Armenian church architecture, the diaspora's unofficial classification of Armenians and dialect differences, and small historic Armenian communities outside Armenia.
one_line: Overview of the Armenian people's religious, political, architectural, and diaspora history.
key_facts: The Armenian collective has at times constituted a Christian "island" in a mostly Muslim region.
A minority of ethnic Armenian Muslims are known as Hamshenis, though many Armenians view them as a separate race.
The history of the Jews in Armenia dates back 2,000 years.
In 1441, Kirakos Virapetsi was elected Catholicos in Etchmiadzin, while Krikor Moussapegiants preserved his title as Catholicos of Cilicia.
Since 1441, there have been two Catholicosates in the Armenian Church with equal rights and privileges and respective jurisdictions.
The primacy of honor of the Catholicosate of Etchmiadzin has always been recognized by the Catholicosate of Cilicia.
Armenia was an independent republic from 1918 to 1920 following the breakup of the Russian Empire.
In late 1920, communists came to power following an invasion of Armenia by the Red Army.
In 1922, Armenia became part of the Transcaucasian SFSR of the Soviet Union.
The Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic existed from 1936 to September 21, 1991.
In 1991, Armenia declared independence from the USSR and established the second Republic of Armenia.
The first Armenian churches were built between the 4th and 7th centuries, beginning with Armenia's conversion to Christianity and ending with the Arab invasion.
By the fifth century the typical central cupola cone had become widely used, and by the seventh century centrally planned churches had been built.
Armenians from Iran are referred to as Parskahay, while Armenians from Lebanon are usually referred to as Lipananahay.
Eastern Armenian in the diaspora is primarily spoken in Iran and European countries such as Ukraine, Russia, and Georgia, where Armenians form a majority in the Samtskhe-Javakheti province.
A community has existed for over a millennium in the Holy Land, and one of the four quarters of the walled Old City of Jerusalem has been called the Armenian Quarter.
An Armenian Catholic monastic community of 35 founded in 1717 exists on an island near Venice, Italy.
